title: All-in-One Augmented Reality Guided Head and Neck Tumor Resection
reviewer_1_strengths: The entire paper is well written, and the novelty of markerless registration for in-situ AR visualization is clearly explained and demonstrated in a thorough evaluation. It is commendable that the evaluation does not only consider technical aspects but also subjective user feedback.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: After reading the document, I wonder how the results presented are to be contextualized in relation to similar work, including markerless approaches. In my opinion, the discussion does not go far enough in this regard. In particular, a connection should be established with the following two aspects, respectively references: Regarding deformable registration (see section on future work): Yang, Q. , Li, F. , Xu, J. , Liu, Z. , Sridhar, S. , Jin, W. , . . . & Wu, J. Y. (2025, September). Augmented Reality-Based Guidance with Deformable Registration in Head and Neck Tumor Resection. In International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention (pp. 45-54). Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. Regarding markerless situs registration: Liebmann, F. , von Atzigen, M. , Stütz, D. , Wolf, J. , Zingg, L. , Suter, D. , . . . & Fürnstahl, P. (2024). Automatic registration with continuous pose updates for marker-less surgical navigation in spine surgery. Medical Image Analysis, 91, 103027. In addition, I spotted redundant information which should be shortened (e. g. , quartile range in the text and in plots), and the statistical reports should be updated according to APA standards (i. e. , including all measures such as effect size). Non-significant aspects should be given less weight, especially given the relatively small sample size. In Figure 3, a significance bar could help to visualize differences, and in Figure 4, the similar color coding for different aspects creates potential for misunderstanding. I recommend that all metrics used should be listed before the Results section; otherwise, the questionnaires used simply appear surprisingly and confuse the reader. Also, the single qualitative quote in the Discussion and Conclusion sections is somewhat surprising; I assume it would be better to have a separate paragraph addressing this feedback within the Results section.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper focuses on specimen re-localization, which is a clinically relevant application scenario that has rarely been addressed in previous AR navigation studies.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Methodological concerns a. Practical usability: specimen deformation and shrinkage Specimen deformation and shrinkage are major issues in the operating room. Although the authors mention these as future work, they are in fact central challenges for any real clinical deployment. Treating the specimen registration problem as rigid severely limits the practical usability of the proposed method. b. Practical usability in iterative resection workflows Re-localization is not a one-time procedure. In real surgical workflows, resection may be iterative. The proposed registration-based strategy appears applicable only to the initially resected specimen and does not seem able to support repeated or iterative re-localization during subsequent resections. c. Depth sensing accuracy of the AHAT camera Previous studies have shown that the depth error of the HoloLens 2 AHAT sensor is substantial and varies across different surface types [Ref 1]. This issue is not considered in the current study, although it may significantly affect both registration accuracy and visualization reliability. d. Dependence on HoloLens SLAM stability The proposed multi-frame stacking approach relies on HoloLens 2 pose estimation, which means that the overall system depends heavily on the stability of the device SLAM for both registration and in-situ visualization. In realistic scenarios, head movement may introduce spatial drift, which could substantially reduce usability and reliability. e. Limited methodological novelty Using a depth camera for point cloud registration has already been widely adopted in previous work [Ref 1]. The pipeline of FPFH-based coarse registration followed by ROI selection and ICP refinement is also a common approach in point-cloud-based registration pipelines [Ref 2]. Registration method difference between this paper and others are not clearly presented. Therefore, the technical novelty of the method itself appears limited, aside from the specific clinical use case. 2.Experimental concerns a. Lack of clarity in the experimental setup The paper does not clearly explain how marker-based registration was performed. As a result, it is difficult to understand the actual difference between the marker-based and markerless registration settings. b. Lack of objective ground truth for registration accuracy Since the authors used a cranial phantom with retro-reflective markers, it should be feasible to establish objective ground truth using CT scanning or an optical scanner. However, no direct objective evaluation of registration accuracy is provided. c. Inappropriate use of expert performance as ground truth The mean performance of experts was used as the ground truth in the evaluation. This is not appropriate for accuracy assessment, because it conflates user error with system error. Ground truth in an accuracy study should be defined independently and objectively. d. Insufficient comparison baseline In Experiment 2, the markerless AR method is compared only with verbal guidance. However, in actual practice, surgeons may also rely on specimen photographs or non-in-situ 3D holographic visualization. These would be more meaningful and clinically relevant baselines for comparison. 3.Writing a. Writing The paper is generally clearly written. However, the comparison with previous studies is insufficient. The manuscript does not clearly articulate its innovation beyond introducing a relatively uncommon use case. b. Figures The figures do not sufficiently illustrate the proposed method. For example, the paper does not clearly show what the AHAT point cloud looks like, how the ROI is extracted, or how the registration pipeline operates in practice. In contrast, there are too many figures dedicated to NASA-TLX and SUS results. Given that only six users were included and limited distribution information is shown, these results could be more effectively summarized in tables rather than multiple separate figures. __ __ __ __ __ __ __ Suggestions for improvement 1.The ground truth should be defined objectively. Expert performance should not be used as the ground truth in an accuracy evaluation. 2.The proposed method should be compared against stronger and more clinically relevant baselines or current standard workflows, rather than only against a very naive verbal-guidance condition. 3.Since the automatic registration procedure occupies a large portion of the method section, if the authors consider automation to be a core contribution, they should: a. clearly explain why automatic registration is particularly important in this application; b. clarify what limitations or ambiguities remain in prior automated approaches; c. provide a clearer demonstration of how the proposed automated method works in practice; d. objectively evaluate the automation result against a non-automated alternative, including both accuracy and efficiency; e. analyze how much time is saved and how much accuracy is preserved over time, particularly under spatial drift or repeated use. __ __ __ __ __ __ __ Reference 1.Li, H., Yan, W., Liu, D., Qian, L., Yang, Y., Liu, Y., … & Wang, G. (2024). EVD surgical guidance with retro-reflective tool tracking and spatial reconstruction using a head-mounted augmented reality device. IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, 31(9), 6497-6511.2.Xiao, Z. (2024, November). ICP Registration Based on Overlapping Region. In 2024 International Conference on Image Processing, Computer Vision and Machine Learning (ICICML) (pp. 980-984). IEEE.
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The proposed technical pipeline successfully removes the workflow burden of manual region-of-interest selection and physical markers. The combination of curvature-biased sampling, TEASER++ for robust global alignment, automatic bounding box construction for cropping, and point-to-plane ICP yields an impressive median TRE of 1.8 mm. 2.The study provides a well-rounded assessment by incorporating human factors. The inclusion of a margin relocation task with six participants, alongside validated workload and usability metrics, strengthens the paper’s claims regarding the system’s practical viability.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The current evaluation is conducted entirely on a rigid silicone face phantom. In actual surgical scenarios, tissue deformation, bleeding, and shrinkage of the resected specimen will heavily impact the rigid surface registration assumptions. 2.The user study relies on a very small sample size of six participants. The absence of experienced attending surgeons limits the generalizability of the baseline “verbal guidance” error.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers. Novelty We agree prior deformable and markerless navigation work needs clearer contrast (R1, R2-1e, R2-3a). Our contribution is an all-in-one AR margin relocalization system using only the HoloLens POV AHAT sensor, without external RGB-D cameras, fiducials, or manual ROI selection (R1, R2-1e). This lowers OR burden by avoiding sensor installation (R1). Yang et al. model deformation but use ArUco and manual landmarks for AR registration [3], and Liebmann et al. study spine navigation with external sensing [4]. R2 Ref.1 concerns AHAT error correction with markers, not markerless specimen-to-bed registration [5]. Our Sec.2 uses curvature-biased sampling, TEASER++-style global alignment, automatic coarse-pose ROI cropping, and ICP for small HN specimens (R2-1e, R3). These choices gave markerless TRE comparable to a marker baseline, median 1.8 mm vs 1.7 mm and max <4 mm (R1, R3). Although we demonstrated our method on HN, our method is broadly applicable to open surgery solid malignancies. Clinical scope We agree deformation and shrinkage are crucial (R2-1a, R3-1). Clinical deployment needs deformation modeling plus markerless AR relocalization of the deformed model (R2-1a). This paper evaluates the second part, still required after deformation modeling (R2-1a). Iterative resections are supported because after any later positive-margin report, the same scan-register-visualize workflow can be rerun (R2-1b). The goal is to reduce repeated re-resections caused by coarse path-to-surgeon communication. [1,2] (R2-1b, R2-2d). Evaluation, ground truth, and baselines We apologize for the wording “expert measurements provided ground truth” (R2-2b, R2-2c). Targets were small physical ink landmarks on the phantom that were also identified on the structured-light specimen model (R2-2b). They were hidden among black marks for blinding participants, while the expert who created them could easily identify them with AR (R2-2c). Expert touching was only a measurement step for known physical landmarks, repeated twice and averaged (for tracking noise), so expert performance was not used as clinical ground truth (R2-2c). The marker baseline used the same STTAR retro-reflective tracking used for the stylus [6] (R2-2a). The study therefore reports registration accuracy versus a fiducial baseline and preliminary margin relocalization accuracy (R2-2d). We agree the phantom task does not capture all intraoperative information, but the verbal script was designed with experienced HN surgeon, and studies show surgeons often rely on verbal pathology communication [1,2] (R2-2d, R3-2). AHAT, SLAM, reporting We agree AHAT error is surface-dependent [5] (R2-1c). In our setup, an AHAT-tracked tool sampled the true local surface contour, nearest depth-sensor points were paired to tool points, and least-squares SVD corrected the local point cloud (R2-1c). This took <30 s and was applied once before experiments (R2-1c). For SLAM, acquisition took ~3s while users viewed the resection bed via AR, followed by noise reduction processing (R2-1d). The ground truth points were also collected right after each experiment to minimize drift. We will streamline statistics and figures, add effect sizes and APA reporting, deemphasize non-significant NASA-TLX and SUS results, clarify experiment setup, and release acquisition, depth correction, and ROI code (R1, R2-3b, R2 reproducibility). [1] Quality in Surgical Pathology Communication and Reporting 2011 [2] How Often Is Cancer Present in Oral Cavity Re-resections After Initial Positive Margins? 2024 [3] Augmented Reality-Based Guidance with Deformable Registration in Head and Neck Tumor Resection 2025 [4] Automatic Registration with Continuous Pose Updates for Marker-less Surgical Navigation in Spine Surgery 2024 [5] EVD Surgical Guidance with Retro-reflective Tool Tracking and Spatial Reconstruction Using a Head-Mounted AR Device 2024 [6] STTAR Surgical Tool Tracking Using Off-the-Shelf AR HMDs 2023
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This submission received mixed and polarizing reviews with two weak-accepts (R1, R3) and one reject (R2). R2 raises various valid concerns, and I recommend that the authors are invited to provide a rebuttal, not only to R2 but also to the concerns raised by R1 and R3.I suggest the authors focus on convincing responses to the critical items: R2 section 7 (1a, 1b, 1c, 1d, 1e, 2b, 2c, 2d, 3a (insufficient SOTA comparison/positioning). The suggestions from the reviewer to improve the paper are valid, however, they constitute major revisions that are not possible post-rebuttal. Consequently, the authors should rebut the critisims based on how the manuscript stands in its current form. R3 section 7, item 1 R1 section 7, novelty issues/positioning regarding 2 refs, and lack of statistical significance reporting. | This submission proposes a markerless AR system for tumor resection guidance. It is based on HoloLens 2 depth sensing, combined with a coarse-to-fine registration pipeline (curvature sampling, FPFH/TEASER++ initialization, ICP refinement). Evaluated was performed on a rigid phantom with a six-participant user study. All reviewers recognize the clinical relevance and the value of eliminating markers and manual ROI selection. R1 and R3 additionally highlight manuscript clarity, automated workflow, user validation, and quantitative improvements over baselines./ R2 also acknowledges good motivation and potential clinical value. The rebuttal clarified key methodological details: landmark-based evaluation, AHAT depth handling, markerless registration baselines, and workflow applicability. However, reviewer concerns about methodological novelty, evaluation rigor, and clinical realism remain post-rebuttal. R2 argues that the method largely follows established depth-based registration pipelines with limited innovation. R2 also raises major issues about rigid phantom evaluation and weak baseline comparisons. R1 and R3 similarly note the small sample size and phantom-only validation l;imitations. In summary, the rebuttal resolved several key issues, and the overall reviewer sentiment shifted positively. I recommend acceptance based on the clinical importance of the problem, the successful integration of a fully markerless AR workflow that removes manual registration steps, supporting evidence from the user validation. Of course, the work remains an early-stage CAI prototype and will require substantially broader validation under realistic clinical conditions, nevertheless, it represents a meaningful contribution. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Following the rebuttal, two reviewers noted that the authors clarified the objective landmark-based evaluation, the markerless registration baseline, AHAT correction procedure, and the intended iterative workflow. However, one reviewer is still concerned regarding deformation and shrinkage, iterative clinical applicability, the appropriateness of the verbal-guidance baseline, and the limited phantom-based evaluation. Overall, while the current study remains preliminary and should more clearly position its contribution relative to prior AR registration work, the rebuttal addressed several major ambiguities and the proposed HoloLens-only workflow demonstrates promising accuracy and translational relevance. I therefore recommend acceptance.

title: EchoVQA: Enabling Conversational Assistance for Point-of-Care Cardiac Ultrasound
reviewer_1_strengths: The dataset fills a critical gap, expanding prior echocardiography VQA resources from only hundreds of QA pairs to a large-scale benchmark with real point-of-care data, significantly enhancing clinical relevance. The inclusion of acquisition-guidance questions is novel, extending VQA from image interpretation to assisting probe operation, directly addressing real-world needs of novice sonographers. The human-in-the-loop data generation pipeline is well-designed, combining expert-defined templates, LLM-based generation, and multi-expert verification to reduce hallucinations and improve reliability. The method is parameter-efficient, achieving near-SOTA performance with only 104M trainable parameters compared to much larger models like LLaVA-Med and LLaVA-Tri. The three-level prompting design is well-validated, with ablations showing complementary contributions from each component rather than redundancy.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The point-of-care data are limited in scale and diversity (≤12 subjects), which weakens claims of generalizability and clinical robustness. The clinical validity of acquisition-guidance QA is not verified, lacking inter-rater agreement or user studies to confirm real-world usability. The expert review process is unclear given the dataset size, with no details on full vs. partial validation or quality control statistics. The methodological contribution is largely compositional, combining existing techniques, and the gains from test-time optimization are marginal relative to its computational cost. The evaluation lacks domain-specific echocardiography baselines and shows limited generalization beyond radiology-heavy settings. Potential dataset bias and incomplete ethical disclosure, along with clarity issues in figures and presentation, further limit reliability and transparency.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The problem this benchmark aims to address is practically motivated. Despite its clinical importance, visual question answering for POCUS remains a largely underexplored area. 2.The question types curated in the benchmark are closely aligned with real-world POCUS interpretation tasks, reflecting strong potential for clinical applicability.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Some additional clarification on the benchmark construction would help readers better understand the design choices. For instance, it would be helpful to explain the rationale behind combining conventional echocardiography from public datasets (EchoNet-Dynamic and CAMUS) with self-collected POCUS images, as well as the key similarities and differences between these data sources. Additionally, since echocardiography is inherently temporal, it would be worth discussing the motivation for using images rather than video clips as input. Finally, as echocardiographic interpretation typically involves multiple views (e.g., A4C, A2C, PLAX, PSAX), clarifying why the benchmark focuses on A4C images — particularly given that existing benchmarks such as MIMIC-Echo-VQA already cover a broader range of views and conditions — would strengthen the paper’s positioning. 2.Further elaboration on the benchmark construction pipeline would help establish its soundness. Specifically, clarifying the relationships among “expert templates,” “category labels,” and “questions” would be beneficial. It would also be helpful to describe how category labels are assigned to each image, how expert templates and category labels interact in the QA generation process, and to provide examples of the resulting QA pairs at each stage. 3.The use of GPT-4o for fine-grained QA generation raises a few points worth addressing. First, given that GPT-4o’s availability may change over time, it would be helpful to discuss contingency plans for reproducing or extending the benchmark when the same model is unavailable. Second, providing some validation or evidence of GPT-4o’s echocardiographic analysis capability would strengthen confidence in the quality of the generated ground-truth annotations, as this is a specialized domain that may benefit from additional scrutiny. 4.The connection between the proposed PEFT strategy and the Echo-VQA benchmark could be made more explicit. The introduction motivates the benchmark by highlighting the scarcity of echocardiography-specific data, yet the PEFT experiments rely on general-purpose medical VQA datasets for training rather than splits derived from Echo-VQA itself. It would be helpful to clarify two related points: first, how the constructed Echo-VQA dataset contributes to MLLM performance improvement, and second, since echocardiographic content appears to constitute a relatively small fraction of the general-purpose training data, what accounts for the observed performance gains on Echo-VQA specifically. 5.The experimental comparisons could be further strengthened by including more recent medical MLLMs, such as MedGemma, Lingshu, and their LoRA fine-tuned variants, to provide a more up-to-date performance reference. In addition, reporting FLOPs for the compared methods would offer a clearer picture of computational costs, since these reflect the parameters actually involved in the optimization process and are important for fair comparison.
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper is easy to follow and impacts the reader from the abstract. All justifications are properly made, and it is clear that authors have thoroughly investigated this field. The work integrates effectively public and private datasets, which resonates to the community that has worked with the former. Authors also clearly understand which are the pains in the medical sector (i.e. sonographers/clinicians not being available at certain times) and all the data acquisition and labelling pipeline has been validated by experts. Every method presented in section 1 is there for a reason, as they have compared and benchmarked against all of them. The sunburst diagram presented in Fig1 is noteworthy, and it is a great example of good practices in visualisation.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The weaknesses I found in the paper are minor, yet I think it is important for me to point them out. In Fig 1, authors could have simply used “im” for images and that could have helped them arrange better the text across the circle. The depiction of step 2 in Fig 2 is a bit confusing; I would have liked to see more detail on how the GPT agent pipelines these steps. Also, I would have liked to see some percentages on how much data is needed from step 1 to help the agent complete the task in 2.In Fig 3 step b, you should have depicted how the question looks like after going through the tokenizer coming into this part of the pipeline. In Table 1, it is unclear why the baseline GPT-4V doesn’t have parameters (I assume because it is a fully closed model) and why it cannot be used in PathVQA and your EchoVQA. References could be standardised better (there are some references that have multiple links and on some you don’t show the conference acronym) and I would have liked to see more references to work previously presented in MICCAI (you only have one workshop paper) to show that you are continuing a trend that interests the people that regularly publish in this venue.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback, and R1/R3 for recognizing EchoVQA as addressing a critical gap. We clarify the dataset pipeline, benchmark scope, and evaluation protocol below. Dataset scope, combining sources, image vs. video, A4C (R1#1, R2#1). EchoVQA spans 14,299 images and 74,819 QA pairs across EchoNet-Dynamic, CAMUS, Lumify, and Clarius, stratified into view-quality categories. The data sources are complementary: the 12-subject PoC subset (7F/5M, age range 23.52–40.57, 3 White / 9 Asian) supplies deployment-like acquisition variation and guidance signal across the non-diagnostic-to-diagnostic spectrum, largely absent from public data, while the public partition adds demographic/pathology breadth from hospital settings. EchoVQA is image-level rather than video-level because acquisition guidance is real-time and frame-specific. Per-image QA is more fine-grained: a clip may begin with LV cutoff and end off-axis, requiring different guidance (“slide medially” vs. “rotate counterclockwise”), while a single video-level instruction would be ambiguous. Image-level guidance therefore provides richer supervision and composes with downstream video LVEF models that assume a diagnostic A4C clip. A4C is the canonical PoC view for LVEF — the most clinically actionable PoC measurement — and one of the hardest for novices to acquire [1,16]; multi-view extension is future work. Expert coverage, IRB, validity (R1#2, R1#3, R1#6). All 74,819 QA pairs were reviewed by 4 experts (Sec. 2.3); given scale, we prioritized full-coverage correctness review over inter-rater agreement on a subset. Guidance was authored or revised by experts following standard acquisition practice [2,16]. A novice-operator user study on guidance efficacy is conducted as separate system-level validation, but was outside this submission. PoC scans collected under IRB (Sec. 2.1). Data/code will be released upon acceptance (R1, R3). QA pipeline (R2#2-#3,R3). Per Sec. 2.2/Fig. 2: experts (i) categorize each image and (ii) author category-specific template QAs, e.g., for A4C_High_Qual: “Can I use this for EF measurement? Yes”, and for A4C_Low_Qual: “Can I estimate EF? No, the view quality is insufficient.”. GPT-4o turns these into image-specific QA capturing within-category variability (LV cutoff, foreshortening, low contrast). Conditioned on category label, templates, and image (not assigning categories) GPT-4o generates pairs like “Q:Can EF be measured? A:No, the LV apex is cut off,” which experts validate for image-grounded correctness.For replication,GPT-4o is not essential;stronger successor MLLMs could reduce expert corrections. Method, baselines, compute (R2#4, R2#5, R1#4–5). Stage 1 (Sec. 3.2) aligns vision–LLM on medical image-caption corpora; Stage 2 fine-tunes per VQA dataset, including EchoVQA splits. Thus EchoVQA gains come from EchoVQA fine-tuning plus EchoVQA-adapted text prompts and TTO (R2#4). Comparisons follow prior per-dataset fine-tuning and strict exact-match/recall metrics (LLaVA-Med, LLaVA-Tri [ICLR 2025], PeFoMed). On echo-specific baselines (R1#5): we agree this would further strengthen the evaluation. Existing echo-specific models such as EchoCLIP and EchoPrime are primarily contrastive/retrieval-style, making direct comparison non-trivial. Still, including them as complementary baselines would indeed have been beneficial for completeness. MedGemma and Lingshu (2025) fold benchmark training splits into generalist multi-stage tuning, so they are not apples-to-apples. Even under Lingshu’s MedEvalKit (LLM-as-judge, looser than our recall), our method exceeds Lingshu-7B and MedGemma-4B-IT on aggregate accuracy (Lingshu Table 6). We report trainable parameters as the optimization-cost proxy and will clarify FLOPs/latency if permitted;TTO adds bounded per-query overhead scaling with vocabulary. We claim not per-component novelty but the medical-VQA-specific combination: visual adaptation prompts, text prompt learning, and TTO.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Reviewers ask for a clearer justification of why conventional echocardiography and self-collected point-of-care data are combined, why the benchmark is image-based rather than video-based, and why the focus is limited to A4C views. They also ask for a much clearer explanation of the QA generation pipeline, including the relationship between expert templates, category labels, GPT-based generation, and expert validation. The number of subjects appears small, and there is not enough evidence yet that the acquisition-guidance questions are clinically valid or useful in practice. Reviewers specifically ask for more detail on subject diversity, expert review coverage, and whether there is any inter-rater agreement or user-level validation. The method contribution seems largely compositional, and about whether the experiments fully leverage the proposed benchmark. Stronger positioning against more recent medical multimodal large language models, together with clearer reporting of computational cost and the role of test-time optimization, would strengthen the paper. These are central enough questions that rebuttal is appropriate before a final decision, and the paper could still move either way depending on how convincingly they are addressed. | Reviewers agree that the clinical problem is important and that the benchmark addresses a meaningful gap in echocardiography-focused VQA. The inclusion of acquisition-guidance questions extends VQA beyond image interpretation toward practical operator assistance. The benchmark itself is the primary contribution of the work, whereas the methodological contribution is generally viewed as incremental and largely compositional. The main concerns relate to the limited size of the POCUS cohort, the absence of user studies or inter-rater agreement analyses for acquisition-guidance questions, and insufficient initial clarity regarding benchmark construction, QA generation, and the rationale for several design choices. The rebuttal provided reasonable clarification regarding dataset composition, expert validation, IRB approval, benchmark scope, and the QA generation pipeline, addressing many of these concerns. While limitations remain regarding dataset diversity, clinical validation, and comparisons with more recent medical multimodal models, these do not outweigh the value of the benchmark contribution. For the camera ready: Clarify benchmark construction and QA generation workflow in greater detail. Improve discussion of limitations arising from the small POCUS cohort. Clearly describe expert review procedures and quality assurance measures. Expand discussion of image-level versus video-level design choices and A4C-only scope. Improve positioning relative to recent medical multimodal large language models and echocardiography-specific methods. Report computational costs and inference overhead associated with test-time optimization. VERY IMPORTANT: All images, QA pairs, expert templates and QA generation prompts must be released under a permissive license and accessible without barriers, e.g. via huggingface or zenodo. Without this the paper would need to be rejected. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper introduces EchoVQA, a clinically motivated benchmark for conversational assistance in point-of-care cardiac ultrasound, together with a parameter-efficient VQA framework. Reviewers found the benchmark timely and clinically relevant, particularly the acquisition-guidance component. Concerns focused on cohort scale, benchmark construction details, and limited evidence for clinical validity and efficiency. The rebuttal clarified the dataset design, QA generation pipeline, and evaluation protocol. While some limitations remain, the overall benchmark contribution and experimental evidence place the paper above the acceptance bar. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I recommend acceptance. Two of the three reviewers support acceptance after the rebuttal. The main contribution, the EchoVQA benchmark with acquisition-guidance questions for point-of-care echocardiography, fills a genuine and underserved gap, and the rebuttal clarified the points the Meta-AC raised. The remaining concerns, including the small 12-subject PoC cohort, the lack of a user study validating acquisition-guidance usefulness, the combination of conventional and PoC data, and the unreported TTO compute cost, are real but reflect requests for additional validation rather than evidence that the results are invalid. I therefore recommend acceptance, with the suggestion that the camera-ready temper generalization claims given the small PoC cohort, clarify the EchoVQA train and test split configuration, and frame the novice-operator user study and FLOPs/latency reporting as necessary follow-up work.

title: MetaFormer: Efficient Metadata-Guided Transformer for Patient-Aware 12-Lead Electrocardiogram Reconstruction
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The problem is defined and of practical significance. Bridging the gap between single-lead wearable devices and clinical 12-lead ECG systems is an important and realistic challenge with strong application value. 2.The paper introduces patient metadata as physiological priors, rather than treating the task as a simple regression problem, which is a meaningful and well-motivated design choice. 3.The paper is well-structured, and the figures are clear and intuitive, making the methodology easy to understand.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The experimental comparisons are not sufficiently comprehensive, as only a limited number of baseline methods are included. 2.The paper does not sufficiently justify the selection of the four metadata attributes, nor does it analyze their individual contributions or explore whether other clinically relevant factors could further improve performance
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Proposed model show great performance: the proposed method outperforms existing approaches while reducing computational cost and adding only minimal additional burden in the form of patient demographic information. The paper is well written, with a clear description of the method and implementation details. The downstream (cardiac diseases classification) evaluation is quite insight full and show the model’s strong potential for clinical application.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The author does not report confidence intervals or standard deviations, which are particularly important when the performance differences relative to the baseline are small. Although the reported metrics (RMSE and PSNR) are useful for model comparison, it would be more clinically interpretable to present errors in ECG features commonly used in diagnosis, such as P-, Q-, R-, S- and T-wave amplitudes, deflections, and intervals.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This work has several strengths in methodology, validation, presentation, and potential relevance. It introduces a metadata tokenizer that can model heterogeneous patient attributes, preserve ordinal structure in continuous variables, and handle missing information through learnable null tokens and simulated dropout. It also designs a metadata-guided cross-attention mechanism that uses patient-specific priors to alleviate cross-lead ambiguity in ECG reconstruction. The overall model is relatively compact and efficient, combining MorphResBlocks with a lightweight Transformer bottleneck to maintain favorable parameter and FLOP cost compared with baseline methods. The experiments cover two large-scale benchmarks, PTB-XL and CSN, and show consistent improvements across multiple reconstruction metrics, including RMSE, PSNR, and CosSim. The ablation studies further examine both metadata injection strategies and tokenizer variants, while the downstream arrhythmia classification results show relatively small gaps compared with original ECGs, supporting the usefulness of the reconstructed signals. The paper is also generally clearly presented: the motivation is easy to follow, the connection between the problem setting and the model design is reasonable, and the method is described with sufficient detail. Overall, the results suggest that metadata conditioning can be a useful way to improve single-lead-to-12-lead reconstruction while keeping the model efficient, and the framework may also be informative for other metadata-informed biosignal or medical inverse problems.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: What are the exact splitting protocols for PTB‑XL and CSN (patient-level vs record-level), and are there any repeated patients across train/val/test? Can you report results with strict patient-level splits to rule out leakage? Which metadata fields are actually available per dataset (e.g., do PTB‑XL/CSN include height/weight), and what is the missingness pattern? What p_drop was used, and how sensitive are results to higher missingness and to incorrect metadata? How is the “resample to a fixed length of 512” implemented relative to the original sampling frequencies and 10 s durations? Are you cropping, downsampling, or segmenting beats? Please clarify the temporal resolution seen by the model and its impact on morphology fidelity. Can you provide per-lead reconstruction metrics and error distributions (e.g., limb vs precordial leads), and per-diagnosis performance deltas in the downstream classifier to identify where metadata helps most? How was the classifier based on [8] adapted to 12‑lead inputs, and what were the training details (architecture, optimizer, epochs, splits)? Are the reported AUC/F1 averaged over multiple runs with confidence intervals? Have you tested cross-dataset generalization (e.g., train on PTB‑XL, test on CSN) and robustness to noise or motion artifacts on the input lead? If so, how does metadata guidance affect robustness? Did you consider adding simple physiological constraints (e.g., Einthoven’s law, Goldberger relations) or vectorcardiographic priors as auxiliary losses? If attempted, how did these interact with the metadata-guided attention? What is the contribution of each metadata attribute individually (age, sex, height, weight)? An ablation per attribute would clarify which priors are most informative for reconstruction.

title: Smartphone-Based ASD Screening via Instance-Adaptive Cross-Modal Fusion and Contrastive Learning
reviewer_1_strengths: The clinical task is well motivated and introduced within the recent state of the art. The methodological challenges to be addressed with respect the state of the art are very clear. At high level, the methodological framework is properly described in each component, as well as the incremental novel technical contributions, properly highlighted by the authors with respect of the recent state of the art for the specific clinical task. Potential real-world clinical impact
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Major points: Code not shared by authors. Lack of ethics considerations for experimental procedures where human subjects are involved in. Lack of ethics protocol approval statement. Minors point: Lack of feedback/references for a possible deployment phase. Lack of standard deviations in 5-fold cross validation experimental results. reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The framework addresses need of combining eye-movement and head-pose modalities for ASD screening. 2.The proposed JRG module is a notable contribution, enabling the model to dynamically and adaptively weight modality-specific contributions on a per-subject basis. This directly addresses the well-known challenge of behavioural heterogeneity in ASD populations, where the relative informativeness of eye-movement versus head-pose signals may vary substantially across individuals. 3.The ablation study in Table 2 is a strong addition, clearly quantifying the contribution of each component of the proposed method.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.While Section 2.1 describes the subject split, no ethical consent declaration is present in the manuscript. For studies involving human participants, particularly a vulnerable population such as children with ASD, this is a critical omission that must be addressed prior to publication. Additionally, the authors should clarify: (a) the clinical basis for ASD and TD categorization (e.g., ADOS scores, formal clinical diagnosis), (b) the specific video stimuli chosen for data collection and the rationale behind this choice, supported by relevant references, and (c) any inclusion/exclusion criteria applied during participant recruitment.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper studies an important and clinically relevant problem. Smartphone-based ASD screening is clearly useful in practice because it could make screening more accessible and easier to deploy at scale than lab-based methods. I also think the paper frames the task well by focusing on unconstrained mobile data collection, where issues like noise, imperfect calibration, and large behavioral variation across children are unavoidable and should be treated as part of the problem. The multimodal setup makes sense for this application. Combining eye-movement and head-pose information is a reasonable design choice, especially since gaze estimates from mobile devices can be noisy and not every child will express ASD-related behaviors in the same way. The eye-movement branch is also well designed. Using fixation heatmaps and scanpath maps is more robust than feeding raw gaze coordinates directly into the model, particularly in a less controlled mobile setting. Joint Representation Gating module is a strong part of the paper. The main idea of letting the model decide how much to rely on each modality for each sample is well matched to the task, since the quality of gaze and head-pose signals can vary a lot from one recording to another. This is also supported by the ablation results, which show that the adaptive fusion strategy works better than simple concatenation, equal weighting, or a single set of learned fusion weights. The paper does a good job with ablations and provides some useful interpretability analysis. The modality, fusion, and loss ablations all support the main argument of the paper. The paper gives good insight into how the adaptive fusion mechanism behaves for ASD versus TD samples.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The main weakness is that the methodological novelty is limited. Both adaptive multimodal gating and supervised contrastive learning are already well established. The contribution is mostly in combining these ideas for smartphone-based ASD screening rather than introducing a genuinely new method. That is acceptable for an application-driven MICCAI paper, but the novelty claims should be stated more carefully. The baseline comparison could also be stronger. While several prior methods are included, it is not fully clear whether they were evaluated under the same preprocessing, splits, and training setup. More importantly, the paper does not compare against stronger generic fusion methods built on the same unimodal encoders, such as cross-attention, FiLM-style fusion, or uncertainty-aware fusion. As a result, it is difficult to determine how much of the gain comes specifically from the JRG module. The evidence for the adaptive fusion claim is also somewhat incomplete. The paper argues that JRG downweights noisy modalities and relies more on stronger signals, which is plausible, but this is not tested directly. A more convincing analysis would corrupt or remove one modality in a controlled way and check whether the learned weights respond as expected. Reproducibility is reasonable but not complete. The overall architecture is described, but some implementation details remain vague, including parts of the contrastive setup, handling of low-confidence gaze points, and parts of preprocessing.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their valuable time and comments. We are encouraged by the positive comments regarding novelty (R1&R2), practical applicability (R1&R3), and experiments/presentation (R2&R3). Ethics Approval (R1&R2): All ethical and experimental procedures were approved by the institutional Medical Ethics Committee and followed the latest version of the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent was obtained from the legal guardians of all child participants before participation. We will clarify the ethics approval and informed consent statement in the manuscript. Reproducibility (R1-R3): We will release the complete code, preprocessing scripts, training configurations, and experimental stimulus videos upon acceptance. These materials will cover supervised contrastive learning, low-confidence gaze handling, gaze/scanpath-map generation, and head-pose preprocessing. De-identified processed eye-movement and head-pose data will also be provided as permitted by ethics approval and informed consent. R1: References for Deployment: AMF-Net only requires a 4-minute video recorded by a mobile-device camera. We have provided supporting references for its key components, including mobile gaze estimation [27], head-pose extraction [1], and supervised contrastive regularization [13]. Standard Deviations: Five-fold standard deviations for Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score are 0.0438, 0.0682, 0.0679, and 0.0454, respectively, showing competitive cross-fold stability. Significance Test/Settings/Metrics: AMF-Net significantly outperforms others under the paired t-test (p<0.05), with 4.97% and 4.06% improvements in Accuracy and F1-score while maintaining a more balanced Precision-Recall trade-off. The main hyperparameters and training settings are provided in Section 3.1, and we follow the same or equivalent metrics and protocols as prior ASD screening studies [4,7,22,26]. R2: ASD/TD grouping was determined using ADOS-2 assessments by qualified clinicians and clinical diagnostic information. The calibration stimuli followed prior gaze-estimation work [27], while the test stimulus concatenated social and geometric scenes (Section 2.1 & Fig. 1), motivated by abnormal preference for geometric stimuli as an ASD biomarker (Pierce et al., Biological Psychiatry, 2016). Inclusion criteria were age 2-8 years and normal/corrected vision; exclusion criteria included age outside this range, inability to cooperate, or visual problems such as strabismus. We will improve Fig. 3 by enlarging fonts/labels and using distinct colors to distinguish the two modalities. R3: Novelty: The main novelty of this work lies in developing an application-oriented model for real-world mobile ASD screening. Based on modality-specific encoding, we adapt and integrate established adaptive multimodal gating and supervised contrastive learning to address practical challenges in unconstrained mobile scenarios, including noisy gaze estimation, large head-pose variations, and inter-subject behavioral heterogeneity. We will refine the contribution statements to better highlight the task-specific adaptation of these components for mobile ASD screening. Fusion Comparison: All compared methods use the same preprocessing, subject-level five-fold split, and training/evaluation settings. We compare AMF-Net with Cross-Attention, FiLM, and Uncertainty-Aware Fusion under the same backbone. They achieve Accuracy/F1-score of 0.8873/0.8848, 0.8797/0.8703, and 0.8870/0.8894, respectively, while AMF-Net achieves 0.9193/0.9206, confirming the effectiveness of JRG. Adaptive Fusion: ASD children have fewer valid eye-movement points than TD children, with Fig. 2 showing lower eye-movement weights for ASD cases. Moreover, modality perturbation experiments reveal that progressive degradation of one modality gradually reduces its weight while raising the other’s weight. These results confirm JRG adaptively adjusts modality contributions by signal reliability.
